We use language-conditioned visual and tactile verifiers, with phase-dependent textual objectives specifying the relevant criteria for each modality. Phase-Dependent Verification Objectives. A single task instruction is often too coarse for long-horizon manipulation: e.g., ℒ \mathcal{L} =“transfer liquid to the blue cup and return” does not explicitly specify intermediate visual objectives (such as moving back to the red cup) or contact requirements (such as squeezing only during dispensing). We therefore use a VLM offline to decompose the task into phase-level textual objectives, { ℓ p } p = 1 P = g VLM ​ ( ℒ ) \{\ell_{p}\}_{p=1}^{P}=g^{\mathrm{VLM}}(\mathcal{L}) , where each phase provides a visual objective ℓ p v \ell_{p}^{v} and a tactile objective ℓ p τ \ell_{p}^{\tau} . The visual verifier determines when to switch to the next phase. Visual Verifier. Visual success depends on if the imagined outcomes appear to be making progress toward the visual objective described in ℓ p v \ell_{p}^{v} . Recent work has developed strong, off-the-shelf, general-purpose reward models that take as input RGB images and textual task descriptions [ 50 , 51 , 52 ] . We leverage these models zero-shot, and we decode our predicted visual latents into RGB image observations o ^ t + H v = 𝒟 φ v ​ ( z ^ t + H v ) \hat{o}^{v}_{t+H}=\mathcal{D}_{\varphi}^{v}(\hat{z}^{v}_{t+H}) and concatenate that with the previous history of observations we have obtained o ≤ t o_{\leq t} as the input of ROBOMETER [ 51 ] reward model for online visual evaluation. This reward is used for long-horizon visual mode selection, where the goal is to distinguish globally meaningful task progress, like moving to the correct cup, mark, or hole. Tactile Verifier. Tactile success depends on fine-grained, often visually ambiguous interactions, such as stable grasping versus incipient slip. We introduce a tactile verifier that is discriminative over subtle contact outcomes, efficient for inference-time evaluation, and flexible to adapt to phase-specific textual contact goals. Specifically, we use a pretrained tactile encoder [ 21 ] with a semantically-aligned latent space and define the tactile reward as the cosine similarity between the phase-level contact description and the tactile embedding: R τ ​ ( z ^ t + h τ , ℓ p τ ) = cos ⁡ ( z ^ t + h τ , ℰ ψ ℓ ​ ( ℓ p τ ) ) , R^{\tau}(\hat{z}^{\tau}_{t+h},\ell_{p}^{\tau})=\cos\left(\hat{z}^{\tau}_{t+h},\mathcal{E}_{\psi}^{\ell}(\ell_{p}^{\tau})\right), where ℰ ψ ℓ ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}_{\psi}^{\ell}(\cdot) is the corresponding text encoder. Computing rewards directly in this latent space makes the verifier discriminative over subtle contact states, efficient for steering without tactile image decoding, and flexible to language-specified contact goals such as “grasp lightly” or “grasp heavily.” To the best of our knowledge, this is the first general-purpose language-conditioned tactile reward. 4.4 Inference-time Optimization for Bi-level Visuo-Tactile Steering Objective At inference time, we solve the bi-level optimization problem from Sec. 4.1 by combining sampling-based visual mode selection with tactile-guided diffusion editing. We describe the implementation details behind this optimization in this section, with further details in Algo. 1 in App. B.3 . Sampling & Verification as Visual Steering. As shown in the inner optimization in Eq. 1 , the visual stage selects a global behavior mode by evaluating long-horizon candidate action sequences. We obtain a set of long-horizon action sequences 𝔸 N = { 𝐚 t : t + H ( i ) ∣ 𝐚 t : t + H ( i ) ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ o t ) } i = 1 N \mathbb{A}_{N}=\{\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H}^{(i)}\mid\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H}^{(i)}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid o_{t})\}_{i=1}^{N} by rolling-out the short action samples obtained from the policy within the world model, decoding the visual observations, passing these into the policy, and repeating. We choose the sequence with the highest visual reward: 𝐚 ¯ t : t + H = arg max 𝐚 t : t + H ∈ 𝔸 N R v ( 𝐳 ^ t : t + H v ; ℓ p v ) . \bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t:t+H}=\arg\max_{\mathbf{a}_{t:t+H}\in\mathbb{A}_{N}}R^{v}\left(\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{v}_{t:t+H};\ell_{p}^{v}\right). Details are in App. B.3 - B.4 . 5 Experiments We evaluate ViTaL on three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks. Our experiments are designed to answer three questions: whether multimodal visuo-tactile steering improves policy over unimodal guidance (Sec. 5.1 ); whether a learned latent world model and semantically aligned verifier provides reliable rewards for predicted outcomes (Sec. 5.2 ); and whether the proposed bi-level optimization balances performance and efficiency compared to naive visual-tactile fusion (Sec. 5.3 ). Robot Setup, Tasks, and Data Collection. We use a Franka Emika robot with RGB and tactile sensors to evaluate ViTaL on three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, including wiping , insertion , and pipette transfer . These tasks require both global visual reasoning, such as selecting the correct mark, hole, or target cup, and local tactile feedback for maintaining contact, resolving alignment, or stabilizing grasp and dispensing behavior. For each task, we collect 50 50 expert demonstrations to train the base diffusion policy π θ \pi_{\theta} with additional 250 250 policy rollouts from intermediate policy checkpoints to train the visuo-tactile world model. Details are in App A . Base Policy. We train a diffusion policy that predicts a 16-step action chunk and executes the first h = 8 h=8 actions at each step. As shown in Fig. 2 , ViTaL outperforms Naive Combination by at least 20 % 20\% across all three tasks. Naive reward fusion often suffers from reward imbalance: the visual objective can dominate selection, leading to actions that appear globally plausible but fail to establish proper contact. Fig. 5 illustrates these failures, where naive fusion can leave orange marks partially wiped, misalign the peg with the hole, or spill liquid. In contrast, ViTaL uses vision to efficiently select globally appropriate behaviors and touch to make targeted local corrections. As detailed in App. D.3 , ViTaL adds 0.05 0.05 second per policy inference step (8 actions) over naive fusion while yielding substantially higher success. These results show that bi-level steering provides a stronger success–speed trade-off. 6 Conclusion We presented ViTaL , a bi-level visuo-tactile inference-time steering framework for contact-rich manipulation. By combining long-horizon visual mode selection with short-horizon tactile refinement in a latent visuo-tactile world model, ViTaL improves performance across three real-world, contact-rich manipulation tasks: pipetting, wiping, and peg insertion. Limitations. Despite the improvement of ViTaL over the base policy, several limitations remain. ViTaL depends on the fidelity of the latent world model, where compounding prediction errors can affect verification, especially for subtle contact events. Its tactile verifier is also limited by tactile encoders pretrained on much smaller datasets than modern VLMs, suggesting that larger-scale tactile pretraining could enable richer contact reasoning.
